🧠 ADHD: Myths vs Facts

ADHD is one of the most misunderstood neurodevelopmental conditions. Unfortunately, myths and misconceptions can delay diagnosis, increase stigma, and prevent individuals from getting the support they need.

❌ Myth: ADHD is caused by poor parenting.
✅ Fact: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition with strong genetic and biological influences.

❌ Myth: Only hyperactive children have ADHD.
✅ Fact: Many individuals, especially girls, may primarily struggle with inattention and organization.

❌ Myth: Children outgrow ADHD.
✅ Fact: While symptoms may change over time, ADHD often continues into adolescence and adulthood.

❌ Myth: ADHD means low intelligence.
✅ Fact: People with ADHD can be highly intelligent, creative, innovative, and successful.

Understanding the facts helps us move away from judgment and toward support, early intervention, and effective treatment.

🚨 Common Signs of ADHD in Children 🚨

ADHD is more than just being energetic or easily distracted. It is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, behavior, emotional regulation, and daily functioning.

Some common signs include:
✔️ Difficulty paying attention
✔️ Excessive fidgeting or restlessness
✔️ Acting without thinking
✔️ Trouble following instructions
✔️ Frequent forgetfulness
✔️ Disorganization
✔️ Easily distracted by surroundings
✔️ Emotional outbursts or frustration

Every child may show some of these behaviors occasionally. However, when these difficulties are persistent, occur across different settings (home and school), and interfere with daily life, a professional evaluation may be helpful.

ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects attention, impulse control, and activity levels. It can impact academic performance, work, relationships, and daily functioning, but with proper understanding and support, individuals with ADHD can thrive.

🔹 Inattentive Type
Often appears as distractibility, forgetfulness, difficulty staying organized, and trouble sustaining attention. These individuals may seem quiet, daydreamy, or “lost in thought.”

Characterized by excessive movement, restlessness, impulsive decisions, frequent interruptions, and difficulty waiting one’s turn.

The most common presentation, involving symptoms of both inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity.

Square Breathing (Box Breathing): A Simple Technique for Panic Attacks

When anxiety or panic starts to rise, square breathing can help slow your breathing and calm your body’s stress response.

⬜ Step 1: Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 2: Hold your breath for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 3: Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 4: Hold your breath again for 4 seconds

Repeat this cycle for 1–3 minutes or until you feel calmer.

Why it helps:
During a panic attack, breathing often becomes rapid and shallow. Square breathing encourages slow, controlled breaths, which can reduce physical symptoms such as a racing heart, dizziness, and feelings of panic.

Remember: Panic attacks are uncomfortable but not dangerous. Controlled breathing can help your body regain a sense of balance and control.

When anxiety or panic starts to rise, square breathing can help slow your breathing and calm your body’s stress response.

⬜ Step 1: Breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 2: Hold your breath for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 3: Breathe out slowly through your mouth for 4 seconds
⬜ Step 4: Hold your breath again for 4 seconds

Repeat this cycle for 1–3 minutes or until you feel calmer.

Why it helps:
During a panic attack, breathing often becomes rapid and shallow. Square breathing encourages slow, controlled breaths, which can reduce physical symptoms such as a racing heart, dizziness, and feelings of panic.

Remember: Panic attacks are uncomfortable but not dangerous. Controlled breathing can help your body regain a sense of balance and control.

If silence triggers anxiety, if thoughts spiral the moment things go quiet, if being alone at night feels genuinely unsettling that is worth exploring.

Watching Someone You Love Struggle Can Bring Up A Strong Urge To Step In And Make Things Better

And sometimes, that urge isn’t just about helping them.
It’s also about how uncomfortable it feels to sit with their pain.

But not everything needs to be fixed immediately.

Some processes take their own time.
And being present, without rushing to solve, can be just as important.

Why " We Need To Talk " Fills You With Dread

"We need to talk" shouldn't feel like a warning.

But when conflict at home was loud, unpredictable, or emotionally unsafe, the nervous system learned to treat it that way.

Some things take a long time to unlearn.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

The Real Reason Queer People Face Mental Health Struggles
Being queer is not a mental health condition.

The distress that queer people experience isn’t caused by being queer. It’s caused by what the world makes of it. The rejection, the concealment, the hypervigilance, the accumulation of being made to feel like you are too much or not enough or simply wrong.

Those are the things that cause harm.

In this conversation, we explore what it actually means to walk into mental health care as a queer person, and why the distinction between identity and experience matters so much in the room.

Head to YouTube to watch the full conversation.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”

Why People Confuse Sex, Gender And Identity

Most people use sex, gender, and sexual orientation interchangeably. They're three distinct things.

Understanding the difference between these three things changes a lot. About how you see yourself. About how you see other people. About why the conversation around identity is more layered than most of us were taught.

In this conversation, we explore what identity actually means, and why collapsing it into a single category leaves so much of the experience unspoken.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

Can Privacy Exist In Healthy Relationship?

Healthy relationships need honesty, but honesty doesn’t always mean immediate or total disclosure.

You’re allowed to process parts of your mental health privately before sharing them. Emotional boundaries are not automatically emotional avoidance.

We often treat openness as an all-or-nothing concept, but emotional safety matters too. Taking time to understand your thoughts, feelings, or triggers before talking about them isn't dishonesty—it's self-awareness.

As Sweta Bothra, Director of Psychology Services at Amaha, reminds us, vulnerability isn't about having no boundaries. It's about sharing from a place of clarity rather than pressure.

3 Ways Grief Comes Back After Loosing A Parent

Why does grief come back years later and feel completely different from the first time?

Here's what no one prepares you for.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

How To Tell A Parent You're Going To Therapy, Without It Turning Into A Fight

"Kya humne kuch galat kiya?"

That's usually where this conversation ends up.

Telling an Indian parent you're going to therapy is its own kind of therapy. Here's how you can navigate it, from the first mention to the moment it gets hard.

Has Your Nervous System Been Trying To Get Your Attention?

The body keeps a record of everything the mind doesn't get a chance to process.

Stress, grief, anxiety, or unresolved things, they don't just disappear because you pushed through them. The body is almost always the first place they show up.

The Biggest Risk With Psychiatric Medications Happens When Someone Starts To Feel Better

A lot of people stop medication when they start feeling better. But psychiatric medication doesn't work that way.

The absence of symptoms is not the same as recovery, and this distinction matters.

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) doesn’t always look like visible rituals
Sometimes, OCD shows up as intrusive thoughts that feel difficult or even impossible to talk about.

These thoughts can centre around harm, religion, or sexuality—often distressing because they go directly against a person’s values.

They’re commonly accompanied by intense guilt, shame, and anxiety, leading people to question their character or keep these experiences to themselves.

But intrusive thoughts in OCD are not a reflection of who someone is.

They are a recognised and well-documented part of the condition.

Understanding this can help reduce shame and make it easier to seek mental health support, therapy, and treatment for OCD.

If this resonates, it might help to know that you’re not alone.

owner_posts.post_text:
Watching Someone You Love Struggle Can Bring Up A Strong Urge To Step In And Make Things Better

And sometimes, that urge isn’t just about helping them.
It’s also about how uncomfortable it feels to sit with their pain.

But not everything needs to be fixed immediately.

Some processes take their own time.
And being present, without rushing to solve, can be just as important.

Why " We Need To Talk " Fills You With Dread

"We need to talk" shouldn't feel like a warning.

But when conflict at home was loud, unpredictable, or emotionally unsafe, the nervous system learned to treat it that way.

Some things take a long time to unlearn.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

The Real Reason Queer People Face Mental Health Struggles
Being queer is not a mental health condition.

The distress that queer people experience isn’t caused by being queer. It’s caused by what the world makes of it. The rejection, the concealment, the hypervigilance, the accumulation of being made to feel like you are too much or not enough or simply wrong.

Those are the things that cause harm.

In this conversation, we explore what it actually means to walk into mental health care as a queer person, and why the distinction between identity and experience matters so much in the room.

Head to YouTube to watch the full conversation.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”

Why People Confuse Sex, Gender And Identity

Most people use sex, gender, and sexual orientation interchangeably. They're three distinct things.

Understanding the difference between these three things changes a lot. About how you see yourself. About how you see other people. About why the conversation around identity is more layered than most of us were taught.

In this conversation, we explore what identity actually means, and why collapsing it into a single category leaves so much of the experience unspoken.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

Can Privacy Exist In Healthy Relationship?

Healthy relationships need honesty, but honesty doesn’t always mean immediate or total disclosure.

You’re allowed to process parts of your mental health privately before sharing them. Emotional boundaries are not automatically emotional avoidance.

We often treat openness as an all-or-nothing concept, but emotional safety matters too. Taking time to understand your thoughts, feelings, or triggers before talking about them isn't dishonesty—it's self-awareness.

As Sweta Bothra, Director of Psychology Services at Amaha, reminds us, vulnerability isn't about having no boundaries. It's about sharing from a place of clarity rather than pressure.

3 Ways Grief Comes Back After Loosing A Parent

Why does grief come back years later and feel completely different from the first time?

Here's what no one prepares you for.

Explore the post—tap “Learn More”.

How To Tell A Parent You're Going To Therapy, Without It Turning Into A Fight

"Kya humne kuch galat kiya?"

That's usually where this conversation ends up.

Telling an Indian parent you're going to therapy is its own kind of therapy. Here's how you can navigate it, from the first mention to the moment it gets hard.

Has Your Nervous System Been Trying To Get Your Attention?

The body keeps a record of everything the mind doesn't get a chance to process.

Stress, grief, anxiety, or unresolved things, they don't just disappear because you pushed through them. The body is almost always the first place they show up.

The Biggest Risk With Psychiatric Medications Happens When Someone Starts To Feel Better

A lot of people stop medication when they start feeling better. But psychiatric medication doesn't work that way.

The absence of symptoms is not the same as recovery, and this distinction matters.

Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) doesn’t always look like visible rituals
Sometimes, OCD shows up as intrusive thoughts that feel difficult or even impossible to talk about.

These thoughts can centre around harm, religion, or sexuality—often distressing because they go directly against a person’s values.

They’re commonly accompanied by intense guilt, shame, and anxiety, leading people to question their character or keep these experiences to themselves.

But intrusive thoughts in OCD are not a reflection of who someone is.

They are a recognised and well-documented part of the condition.

Understanding this can help reduce shame and make it easier to seek mental health support, therapy, and treatment for OCD.

If this resonates, it might help to know that you’re not alone.

owner_posts.post_text: Phone addiction has become one of the biggest parenting challenges today. Parents struggle with setting boundaries, managing constant conflicts, monitoring online safety and competing with the appeal of screens. Many also feel guilty because they use phones themselves. The goal is not to eliminate technology, but to teach children balance, responsibility and healthy digital habits.

Growing up, many of us were taught that parents are the safest people to talk to. But sometimes children don’t need advice, solutions, or life lessons — they just need to feel heard. When emotions are dismissed often enough, silence slowly starts feeling safer than honesty. And what looks like distance is sometimes just someone protecting parts of themselves that once felt misunderstood.

Sometimes I wonder how a person can be considered “too young” to fully understand consequences, yet old enough to commit something so horrific. It’s difficult to balance accountability with the belief that people can change.

We often underestimate how stressed corporate professionals can be. Long hours, constant deadlines, endless notifications, pressure to always perform, and the inability to truly switch off slowly take a toll. Just because someone is sitting in an office, dressed well, and functioning normally does not mean they are mentally okay. Think about it.
Yet another time with one of my favourites,

Working with Godrej has always been a fun-filled experience—each time they come up with something unique that has a psychological tinge to it. This time, we explored how safe spaces actually change our perceptions and perspectives. 

Hyderabad was fun.
Another city coming soon.

Children today are growing up inside powerful digital systems that shape attention, self-worth and emotional safety. Instead of reacting with outrage or blanket bans, the conversation must centre on protection. Thoughtful guardrails and digital literacy can help young people build resilience before stepping into a world designed to capture them.

I am often asked, “In a room full of testosterone, does your cortisol soar?”
Well, no but my dopamine certainly does. And toward the end, my serotonin spikes too. The only one periodically off the charts is insulin -  but yes, oxytocin will always be my favourite.
